prompt: What kind of product forms when Br2 or Cl2 adds to an alkene?

choices.text: A 1,2-dihalide, with one halogen on each former double-bond carbon
A 1,1-dihalide, with both halogens on the same former double-bond carbon
choices.why: Halogenation puts one halogen on each of the two double-bond carbons.

choices.text: An alkyl halide with just one halogen atom, plus a molecule of HX
choices.why: Both halogen atoms of X2 end up in the product; no HX forms.

choices.text: A halohydrin, with a halogen on one carbon and an −OH on the other
choices.why: That needs water present to act as a nucleophile. With X2 alone, the product is a 1,2-dihalide.

explanation: Bromine and chlorine add rapidly to alkenes to yield 1,2-dihalides, a process called halogenation. Ethylene and Cl2, for example, give 1,2-dichloroethane.

prompt: Why are fluorine and iodine rarely used to halogenate alkenes?

choices.text: Fluorine is too reactive and difficult to control, and iodine does not react with most alkenes
Iodine is too reactive and difficult to control, and fluorine does not react with most alkenes
choices.why: This swaps them. Fluorine is the overly reactive one; iodine is the unreactive one.

choices.text: Both react only through carbocations and so give cis/trans mixtures
choices.why: The reasons given are fluorine's high reactivity and iodine's lack of reactivity, not the mechanism.

choices.text: Both are far too expensive and too hard to obtain for laboratory use
choices.why: Cost isn't the reason given. Fluorine is too reactive to control and iodine doesn't react with most alkenes.

explanation: Br2 and Cl2 add rapidly to alkenes. Fluorine is too reactive and difficult to control for most laboratory applications, and iodine does not react with most alkenes.

prompt: What is the product of adding Cl2 to ethylene, H2C=CH2?

choices.text: 1,2-Dichloroethane, ClCH2CH2Cl
1,1-Dichloroethane, CH3CHCl2
choices.why: Each chlorine bonds to a different carbon of the former double bond.

choices.text: Chloroethylene (vinyl chloride), H2C=CHCl
choices.why: Addition turns the double bond into a single bond, but chloroethylene still has a C=C bond.

choices.text: Chloroethane, CH3CH2Cl
choices.why: That would come from adding HCl. Adding Cl2 puts a chlorine on each carbon.

explanation: Cl2 adds across the double bond to give 1,2-dichloroethane (ethylene dichloride). Nearly 50 million tons are made worldwide each year, much of it this way, for use as a solvent and as a starting material for PVC.

prompt: About how many million tons of 1,2-dichloroethane are synthesized worldwide each year?
explanation: Nearly 50 million tons of 1,2-dichloroethane (ethylene dichloride) are made each year, much of it by adding Cl2 to ethylene. It is used as a solvent and to manufacture poly(vinyl chloride), PVC.

prompt: What is formed when Br2 adds to cyclopentene?

choices.text: trans-1,2-Dibromocyclopentane only
cis-1,2-Dibromocyclopentane only
choices.why: cis-1,2-Dibromocyclopentane is not formed. The two bromines add from opposite faces.

choices.text: A mixture of cis- and trans-1,2-dibromocyclopentane
choices.why: A mixture is what a planar carbocation intermediate would give, but only the trans isomer is observed.

choices.text: 1,1-Dibromocyclopentane only
choices.why: Each bromine bonds to a different carbon of the former double bond.

explanation: Halogenation of a cycloalkene gives only the trans dihalide. Bromination of cyclopentene gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclopentane as the sole product, a result of anti addition through a bromonium ion.

prompt: Halogenation of cyclopentene occurs with anti stereochemistry. What does that mean?

choices.text: The two halogen atoms come from opposite faces of the double bond
The two halogen atoms come from the same face of the double bond
choices.why: That would give the cis product. Anti means one halogen comes from the top face and one from the bottom.

choices.text: The halogen adds to the carbon with fewer alkyl substituents
choices.why: That would be about which carbon gets which group, not about the faces the atoms come from.

choices.text: The two halogen atoms end up on the same carbon
choices.why: Each halogen bonds to a different carbon; anti refers to the faces they arrive from.

explanation: Anti stereochemistry means the two bromine atoms come from opposite faces of the double bond, one from the top face and one from the bottom. On a ring, this gives the trans product.

prompt: Why is a simple carbocation mechanism not consistent with the bromination of cyclopentene?

choices.text: A planar carbocation would give both cis and trans dibromides, but only trans forms
A carbocation would give only the trans dibromide, but the cis isomer forms
choices.why: It's the reverse: only the trans isomer forms, and a planar carbocation would allow both.

choices.text: Br2 cannot act as an electrophile toward the electron-rich double bond
choices.why: The accepted bromonium mechanism still begins with electrophilic addition of Br+ to the alkene.

choices.text: A carbocation mechanism would put both bromine atoms on the same carbon
choices.why: Both mechanisms put one bromine on each carbon. The problem is the stereochemistry.

explanation: A carbocation intermediate is planar, so Br− could attack from either face, giving a mixture of cis and trans isomers. Because cycloalkenes give only the trans dihalide, that mechanism doesn't account for the observed stereochemistry.

prompt: According to Kimball and Roberts, what is the intermediate in the addition of Br2 to an alkene?

choices.text: A cyclic bromonium ion, with a positive bromine bonded to both carbons
A planar carbocation, with a bromine on the neighboring carbon
choices.why: That was the first, plausible mechanism, but it doesn't explain the anti stereochemistry.

choices.text: A carbon radical, formed by adding a single bromine atom
choices.why: Halogenation is a polar electrophilic addition; its intermediate is a cation, not a radical.

choices.text: A carbanion, formed by adding a bromide ion to the alkene
choices.why: The intermediate is positively charged. Br− is released as it forms and attacks it in the second step.

explanation: In 1937 George Kimball and Irving Roberts proposed that the intermediate is not a carbocation but a bromonium ion, R2Br^+, formed in a single step as the alkene interacts with Br2 and Br− is lost. Bromide ion then opens it in the second step.

prompt: How does a bromonium ion intermediate explain the trans product from cyclopentene?

choices.text: The bromine shields one face, so Br− attacks from the opposite, unshielded face
Br− attacks from the same face as the bromine, which attracts it
choices.why: The large bromine blocks that face, so attack comes from the opposite side.

choices.text: The ring flips after addition, converting the cis product into trans
choices.why: The trans product forms directly in the second step; no cis product is converted.

choices.text: The bromonium ion is planar, so Br− attacks either face equally
choices.why: Equal attack on both faces would give a cis/trans mixture. The bromine of the bromonium ion shields one face.

explanation: If a bromonium ion forms, the large bromine atom shields one side of the molecule. Br− can then react only from the opposite, unshielded side, giving trans-1,2-dibromocyclopentane.

prompt: A chloronium ion has the general formula R2Cl^+. How many bonds does its positively charged chlorine form?
explanation: A chloronium ion contains a positively charged, divalent chlorine. Like the bromine in a bromonium ion, it is bonded to both carbons of the former double bond.

prompt: How do haloperoxidase enzymes in marine organisms bring about alkene halogenation?

choices.text: They use H2O2 to oxidize Br− or Cl− to a biological equivalent of Br+ or Cl+
They reduce Br2 or Cl2 to halide ions, which then add to the double bond
choices.why: It's the other way around: the enzymes oxidize halide ions to a Br+ or Cl+ equivalent, the electrophile.

choices.text: They generate halogen radicals, which add to the double bond in a chain
choices.why: The biological route forms a bromonium or chloronium ion, just as in the laboratory.

choices.text: They protonate the double bond, and the carbocation captures a halide
choices.why: The biological route goes through a bromonium or chloronium ion, not a carbocation.

explanation: Biological halogenations, found mainly in marine organisms living in halide-rich environments, are carried out by haloperoxidases. These use H2O2 to oxidize Br− or Cl− to a biological equivalent of Br+ or Cl+. Electrophilic addition gives a bromonium or chloronium ion, and another halide ion completes the reaction. Halomon, an antitumor compound from red alga, is thought to form this way.

prompt: What product would you expect from adding Cl2 to 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene?

choices.text: trans-1,2-Dichloro-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane
cis-1,2-Dichloro-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane
choices.why: Halogen addition is anti, so the two chlorines end up trans on the ring.

choices.text: A mixture of cis- and trans-1,2-dichloro-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane
choices.why: Addition through a chloronium ion gives only the trans product, just as cyclopentene gives only the trans dibromide.

choices.text: 1-Chloro-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane
choices.why: That would come from adding HCl. Cl2 puts a chlorine on each double-bond carbon.

explanation: Cl2 adds through a chloronium ion, and Cl− attacks from the opposite face. Each former double-bond carbon gets one chlorine, trans to each other: trans-1,2-dichloro-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane.

prompt: Adding HCl to 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene gives two stereoisomers of 1-chloro-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, but adding Cl2 gives only one stereoisomer of its product. Why the difference?

choices.text: HCl's carbocation can be attacked on either face; Cl2's chloronium ion only on the opposite face
HCl goes through a chloronium ion, while Cl2 goes through a planar carbocation
choices.why: It's the reverse. Halonium ions form from X2; HCl addition goes through a carbocation.

choices.text: Cl2 reacts much faster than HCl, so it has no time to form a second stereoisomer
choices.why: The difference lies in the intermediate, not the speed. Only a halonium ion shields one face.

choices.text: HCl adds with anti stereochemistry, while Cl2 adds with syn stereochemistry
choices.why: Cl2 adds anti. HCl gives a mixture because its planar carbocation can be attacked from either face.

explanation: A planar carbocation can react from either face, giving a mixture of isomers, which is exactly what the section says a carbocation mechanism would predict. A chloronium ion shields one face, so Cl2 gives only the trans product.

prompt: What product would you expect from adding Br2 to cyclohexene?

choices.text: trans-1,2-Dibromocyclohexane
cis-1,2-Dibromocyclohexane
choices.why: Bromination of a cycloalkene is anti, giving the trans isomer, just as cyclopentene gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclopentane.

choices.text: A 50:50 mixture of cis- and trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane
choices.why: A mixture would be expected from a planar carbocation, but the bromonium ion gives only trans.

choices.text: Bromocyclohexane
choices.why: That would come from adding HBr. Br2 puts a bromine on each double-bond carbon.

explanation: As with cyclopentene, a bromonium ion forms and Br− attacks it from the opposite face, so the only product is trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.

prompt: What is the product of adding Br2 to 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2?

choices.text: 1,2-Dibromo-2-methylpropane, (CH3)2CBrCH2Br
1,1-Dibromo-2-methylpropane, (CH3)2CHCHBr2
choices.why: Halogenation gives a 1,2-dihalide: one Br on each former double-bond carbon.

choices.text: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CBr
choices.why: That is the product of HBr addition. Br2 adds two bromine atoms.

choices.text: 1-Bromo-2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CHBr
choices.why: Addition removes the double bond, but this compound still has a C=C bond.

explanation: Br2 adds one bromine to each carbon of the double bond, giving the 1,2-dibromide (CH3)2CBrCH2Br, named 1,2-dibromo-2-methylpropane.
